design_detail: Secondary analysis of the Euro-DEN Plus Registry, a multicentre registry of consecutive emergency department (ED) presentations with acute recreational or illicit drug toxicity at sentinel hospitals in Europe, 1 October 2013 to 31 December 2016 (22 EDs in 14 countries took part in this analysis; 18 contributed patients). Patients with acute toxicity from GHB, GBL or 1,4-butanediol (pooled as GHB/GBL) and no other drug were split by report of ethanol co-ingestion into Group A (GHB/GBL alone, n = 183) and Group B (GHB/GBL with ethanol, n = 426). Case and ethanol status were taken from the patient or companions, the attending physician or toxicology at the physician's discretion; each centre's principal investigator adjudicated cases with no central review. Nineteen predefined clinical features, ED management and outcome were compared with chi-square or Fisher tests, t tests and unadjusted odds ratios from univariable logistic regression; no multivariable model. Read as the journal's accepted manuscript (one named author; not the typeset article).
can_establish: How reported ethanol co-ingestion went with the clinical features, treatment, disposition and hospital stay of 609 ED patients who had taken GHB/GBL and no other drug, as unadjusted comparisons across 18 European centres.
cannot_establish: That ethanol caused the differences; effects at known amounts or concentrations of either drug; risk in people who do not reach an ED; whether breathing is affected (slow breathing, oxygen saturation and intubation were not detectably different, with wide intervals and about one in five breathing rates missing); or which single difference would survive correction for the more than 30 unadjusted comparisons.

sample.recruitment: Registry: Euro-DEN Plus sentinel EDs, consecutive presentations with acute recreational or illicit drug toxicity, entered on a purpose-designed minimum dataset; the network began in 2013 with a European Commission grant and had 32 centres in 21 countries by the end of 2017; investigators meet about yearly to harmonise inclusion; case adjudication by each centre's principal investigator, with no external or central review (Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: acute toxicity related to GHB/GBL, alone or with ethanol, when the patient or companions reported GHB/GBL use, or the attending physician reported the presentation as related, or toxicology at the physician's discretion confirmed GHB/GBL and no other drug except ethanol; the same sources decided ethanol co-ingestion. Excluded: presentations with any other drug, and (Fig 1) 467 GHB/GBL presentations with no data on ethanol (Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Age 32.0 years (SD 8.4; 10 missing); women 19.0% (81% men). Group A against Group B: age 33.1 (7.9) against 31.5 (8.5), P = 0.029; women 16.4% against 20.2%, P = 0.274; arrival by ambulance 68.3% against 86.6%, P < 0.001 (Table 2). Race, ethnicity, setting, time since ingestion and medical history are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registry), but 467 of 2,349 patients with GHB/GBL involvement (19.9%, editors' calculation) had no ethanol data and were excluded. Missing values in the analysed 609: temperature 54.4%, respiratory rate 20.7%, blood pressure 18.6%, Glasgow Coma Score 9.5%, heart rate 7.7%, age 1.7% (Table 2); how missing values were handled is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Only patients who reached an ED at 18 centres: six centres provide 93% of the patients (editors' arithmetic from Table 1: two London centres 297, two Oslo centres 209, Tallinn 33, Barcelona 26), so the series reflects London and Oslo practice and patients; one Oslo centre is an accident and emergency outpatient clinic. The share with ethanol differs by centre (54% to 86% in the six large centres, editors' calculation), and the threshold for calling an ambulance, attending an ED, admitting to critical care or giving sedatives may differ by centre and by whether alcohol is known to be involved. People managed before the ED, and those who died before arrival, are not in the registry; 67.6% of GHB/GBL patients with ethanol data (1,273 of 1,882) had other drugs and are excluded, so the analysed patients are a minority of GHB/GBL presentations (Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Fig 1; Table 1).

exposure.measurement: Report by the patient or companions, report by the attending physician, or toxicology at the physician's discretion, with the same criteria for GHB/GBL and for ethanol. Toxicology was done in 38 patients (6.2%) in a minority of centres and found GHB/GBL in 28.9% of them (11 of 38, editors' arithmetic), which the author attributes to the short detection window (Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Table 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: no amount of GHB, GBL, 1,4-butanediol or ethanol, no time since ingestion, no product or route; ethanol is a yes/no report and the three GHB-related compounds are pooled.
exposure.polysubstance: Excluded by design: 1,273 presentations with other drugs (cathinones, methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine, opiates, cannabis, MDMA, ketamine, poppers; Fig 1). The author says unreported or unanalysed co-ingestion cannot be excluded and cites earlier work showing high agreement between admitted use and toxicology; the authors also say excluding other drugs may have biased the intubation estimate towards a lower rate (Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).

comparison.controls: Group A, patients with GHB/GBL toxicity and no reported ethanol (n = 183) at the same centres.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Amount and timing of each drug, regular use and tolerance, circumstances (the author names sexualised drug use, chemsex, as one that may differ by area), time between ingestion and arrival, and medical and psychiatric history are not recorded or not reported (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other drugs excluded by design; unreported co-ingestion unmeasured. No adjustment for age, sex or centre.

outcomes.instruments: Nineteen predefined clinical features recorded in routine ED care (reduced consciousness as a Glasgow Coma Score below 13; bradycardia below 60 and tachycardia above 100 beats per minute; bradypnoea below 12 and tachypnoea above 20 breaths per minute; hypothermia below 35 and hyperthermia above 39 degrees C; systolic pressure below 90 or above 180 mm Hg; vomiting, seizures, agitation and others), ED treatment, disposition, length of stay and death (Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated in this paper; features recorded by the treating team, with the time of measurement not given (the Discussion says features refer to the whole ED stay).
outcomes.operationalization: Percentage of patients with each feature among those with data; critical care admission as a share of patients hospitalised; length of stay in hours.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 33 between-group comparisons are reported in Tables 2 and 3 (21 in Table 2, 11 in Table 3, and death) and three within-group intubation comparisons; the author notes only the risk of missing real differences (beta error).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: clinicians recorded features, gave sedatives and decided on admission knowing the history, including alcohol.

analysis.effect_sizes: Group A (GHB/GBL alone, n = 183) against Group B (with ethanol, n = 426); odds ratios unadjusted, from univariable logistic regression. Decreased consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13) 49.1% against 58.9% (P = 0.034 in Results and Table 2; 0.031 in the Abstract), OR 1.490 (1.029 to 2.158), 309 of 551 patients with data. Bradycardia 23.5% against 15.7% (P = 0.027), OR 0.604 (0.386 to 0.948). Bradypnoea 11.6% against 8.2% (P = 0.246; 20.7% missing); tachypnoea 14.0% against 14.7% (P = 0.839); vomiting 10.3% against 15.0% (P = 0.129); seizures 6.9% against 7.2% (P = 0.675); agitation 34.9% against 33.1% (P = 0.679); hypotensive episode 1.5% against 2.2% (P = 1.00); arrhythmia 1.2% against 0.8% (P = 0.645). Fig 2 (unadjusted odds ratio for ethanol co-ingestion, 95% CI; read on the rendered page): headache 1.711 (0.477 to 6.141); vomiting 1.536 (0.880 to 2.683); hallucinations 1.496 (0.486 to 4.611); decreased level of consciousness 1.490 (1.029 to 2.158); hypotensive episode 1.461 (0.306 to 6.968); hypothermia 1.365 (0.657 to 2.839); chest pain 1.272 (0.254 to 6.365); anxiety 1.258 (0.723 to 2.19); seizures 1.165 (0.570 to 2.380); tachypnoea 1.071 (0.601 to 1.910); tachycardia 1.019 (0.619 to 1.676); agitation or aggressive behaviour 0.924 (0.637 to 1.341); psychotic signs and symptoms 0.735 (0.212 to 2.544); bradypnoea 0.684 (0.354 to 1.322); arrhythmias 0.663 (0.110 to 4.003); bradycardia 0.604 (0.386 to 0.948); palpitations 0.555 (0.190 to 1.624); hypertensive episode 0.498 (0.155 to 1.597). Management (Table 3): any treatment 49.2% against 60.4% (P = 0.011); sedative drugs 12.8% against 20.1% (P = 0.034); orotracheal intubation 3.9% against 5.9% (P = 0.321; 32 of 609 overall, 5.3%); naloxone 19% against 21.5% (P = 0.495); flumazenil 3.4% against 3.4% (P = 0.703). Disposition: discharge 63.4% against 64.1% and hospitalisation 36.6% against 35.7% (P = 0.842); among patients hospitalised (219), critical care 15 of 67 (22.4%) against 84 of 152 (55.3%) and medical ward 76.1% against 43.4% (P < 0.001); as shares of all patients in each group, critical care 8.2% against 19.7% (editors' calculation). Median time in hospital 2 h 18 min (IQR 1:01 to 4:11) against 3 h 11 min (1:56 to 7:13), P < 0.001; more than 6 hours 16.9% against 28.4% (P = 0.003). Deaths: 0 against 2 (0.5%), P = 1.00. Intubation by Glasgow Coma Score: 0.7% at 15, 2.1% at 8 to 14, 14.5% below 8 (P < 0.001); not related to vomiting (6.3% against 5.3%) or seizures (7.5% against 5.3%). Editors' rough calculation from the printed counts and percentages for intubation: odds ratio about 1.5 with a 95% interval of about 0.7 to 3.7. Table 1 counts by centre, editors' arithmetic: the share of patients with ethanol in the six centres with more than 25 cases runs from 54% (Oslo accident and emergency outpatient clinic, 75 of 139) and 58% (Tallinn, 19 of 33) to 76% (Guy's and St Thomas', 188 of 246), 82% (King's College, 42 of 51) and 86% (Oslo University Hospital, 60 of 70).
analysis.covariates: None: univariable comparisons only, with no adjustment for age, sex, centre, time of presentation or any other variable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A secondary analysis of a registry; no protocol or registration for this analysis is mentioned. The 19 clinical features are described as predefined in the registry's minimum dataset.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 19 features appear in Table 2 and 18 in Fig 2 (none had hyperthermia); the Abstract and Highlights feature the significant differences. Some Abstract values do not match the Results and tables (consciousness P = 0.031 against 0.034; ages labelled Group A/B as 31.5/33.1 when Table 2 gives A 33.1 and B 31.5; consciousness and sedatives listed B/A while the other pairs are A/B). No correction for about 33 comparisons.
analysis.power: Not calculated; the author states some features were too infrequent to detect differences (beta error). Intervals for the rare features (hypotension, arrhythmia, chest pain, seizures) are very wide (Fig 2).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 609 ED patients with GHB/GBL toxicity and no other drug, those reported to have taken ethanol (Group B) arrived by ambulance more often (86.6% against 68.3%), were younger (31.5 against 33.1 years) and were recorded with a Glasgow Coma Score below 13 more often (58.9% against 49.1%; OR 1.49, 1.03 to 2.16), were given any treatment (60.4% against 49.2%) and sedatives (20.1% against 12.8%) more often, and, among those hospitalised, went to critical care more often (55.3% against 22.4%); they stayed longer (median 3 h 11 min against 2 h 18 min). Bradycardia was less frequent (15.7% against 23.5%). No difference was detected in slow or fast breathing, seizures, vomiting, other features, intubation (5.9% against 3.9%), antidotes or overall disposition. Two patients died, both in Group B. All comparisons are unadjusted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Highlights and Conclusions say co-ingestion of ethanol increases the adverse effects in patients intoxicated by GHB/GBL, leading to greater depression of consciousness, need for treatment, admission to the ICU and longer hospital stay, and the Conclusions call the results first evidence about the influence of ethanol on the clinical profile. Gaps: (1) increases states a causal effect, from unadjusted comparisons in which the groups differ in age, mode of arrival and centre mix, and exposure rests on report; (2) depth of depression of consciousness is not measured, only the share below a Glasgow Coma Score of 13 (9.5% missing); (3) the critical care percentages are shares of patients hospitalised (22.4% and 55.3%), not of all patients (8.2% and 19.7%), and the Abstract does not give the denominator; (4) about 33 uncorrected comparisons with a borderline P = 0.034 for the main clinical feature; (5) no difference in intubation or breathing features is described as no difference, with wide intervals and a possible downward bias the author names; (6) first evidence overlooks a controlled volunteer experiment of ethanol with GHB (not cited).

timeline.event: Thai et al. (J Clin Psychopharmacol): a randomized double-blind crossover study in 16 healthy volunteers; ethanol with GHB lowered oxygen saturation by a little more than either alone (about 2 points at the largest mean fall); a different design and outcome; not cited in this paper; read for this library.
Liechti et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend): clinical features of GHB and GBL toxicity and concomitant drug and alcohol use, cited here as background; not read.
Miro et al. (Toxicology Letters): same registry, pure GHB intoxication compared with that combined with other substances, cited as background; not read.
This paper: ED patients with GHB/GBL alone or with ethanol, unadjusted comparisons.

replication.where_it_stands: In direction, the two sources read for this library agree: ethanol with GHB went with more sedation or physiological effect (more reduced consciousness and critical care use in patients; a small extra fall in oxygen saturation in volunteers). They measure different outcomes at unrecorded (patients) or fixed (volunteers) amounts, neither is large enough or adjusted enough to size the risk, and no study read measured both drugs in the blood of patients. A later independent analysis was not found among the sources read.

funding.funder: No funding statement for this analysis. The Euro-DEN network was funded by a European Commission grant (JUST/2012/DPIP/AG/3591) in 2013 to 2015 (Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 1st paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships (Declaration of interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Hospital Clinic Barcelona (corresponding author); the registry is run by the Euro-DEN Plus research group. The accepted manuscript names one author. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A registry or prospective analysis that records the amount and time of GHB/GBL and ethanol, measures both in blood, adjusts for centre, age, sex and other recorded drugs, uses fixed rules for the timing of Glasgow Coma Score, breathing rate and oxygen saturation, and defines critical care admission by criteria that do not depend on knowing about alcohol; for breathing, controlled studies in volunteers with continuous measurement at graded alcohol exposure, as far as ethics allow.

domains.note: Univariable comparisons only. The groups differ in age and mode of arrival and probably in centre mix, amounts taken, regular use, setting and time since ingestion; none is adjusted for.

Ethanol (and GHB/GBL) status rests on report by the patient, companions or the physician; toxicology in 6.2%, detecting GHB/GBL in 28.9% of those; no amounts or times. Patients with reduced consciousness may be less able to give a history, so unreported ethanol in Group A is plausible and may be related to severity.

ED attendance only, 93% from six centres and 83% from London and Oslo; 467 presentations without ethanol data excluded; 67.6% of the rest excluded for other drugs; the threshold for attendance, ambulance use and admission may differ with alcohol.
Treatment and admission are also outcomes here and depend on local practice and on knowing alcohol was involved.
Temperature missing in 54.4%, respiratory rate 20.7%, blood pressure 18.6%, Glasgow Coma Score 9.5%; complete-case percentages, handling not described.

Predefined features recorded in routine care with unstated timing; Glasgow Coma Score cut-off is a reasonable marker, but sedative use, treatment and critical care admission depend on clinicians who knew the history.
A secondary analysis with no protocol mentioned; all predefined features are shown; about 33 comparisons without correction; Abstract values differ from the tables in places.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and four domains are judged high (confounding, exposure measurement, selection and missing data). The series is large for GHB/GBL, covers several countries, excludes other drugs by design and shows all predefined features, and the direction of the main differences is plausible. It may be cited for the unadjusted differences between reported ethanol co-ingestion and no co-ingestion in ED patients (consciousness, treatment, critical care, stay), for the absence of a detected difference in breathing features and intubation with wide intervals, and for the two deaths; not for a causal increase, for any amount or concentration, for breathing risk, or for risk in people who do not attend an ED.

key_findings.finding: Aim and design: to study the clinical impact of ethanol co-ingestion in patients presenting to the ED with acute GHB/GBL toxicity. Secondary analysis of the Euro-DEN Plus Registry (14 countries, 22 EDs; 17,371 consecutive patients with acute recreational drug toxicity over 39 months, October 2013 to December 2016): lone GHB/GBL (Group A) against GHB/GBL with ethanol (Group B), without other drugs.

Case definition: GHB/GBL toxicity was diagnosed from clinical history and/or data collected during emergency care; a case was included when the patient or companions reported GHB/GBL use, or the attending physician reported the presentation as related, or toxicology at the physician's discretion confirmed GHB/GBL and no other drug except ethanol; the same factors decided ethanol co-ingestion; presentations with other drugs were excluded. Case adjudication by each centre's principal investigator, with no external or central review.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 2nd paragraph; Study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Data and tests: demographics, 19 predefined clinical features, ED management and outcome (disposition, length of stay, death), and toxicology when done; chi-square (or Fisher) and t tests, and the association of ethanol with each feature estimated univariately as an odds ratio by logistic regression; P below 0.05 or an interval excluding 1 counted as significant.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Flow: 17,371 registry patients; 15,022 without GHB/GBL; 2,349 (13.5%) with GHB/GBL; 467 without ethanol data; 1,882 with ethanol data, of whom 183 (9.7%) were Group A, 426 (22.6%) Group B and 1,273 (67.6%) had other drugs and were not included. Four of the 22 centres included no patient; six centres with more than 25 cases each supplied 93% (565 of 609; the two London centres 297 and the two Oslo centres 209, editors' arithmetic from Table 1).
key_findings.note: Fig 1 and Table 1 were checked on the rendered pages; the counts by centre add to 609.

key_findings.finding: Patients: mean age 32.0 years (SD 8.4), 81% men; Group B were younger (31.5 against 33.1 years, P = 0.029) and arrived by ambulance more often (86.6% against 68.3%, P < 0.001); no difference by sex.

Clinical features: the most common was reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13) in 56.1% (309; 58 missing), more frequent in Group B (58.9% against 49.1%, P = 0.034; Abstract P = 0.031); the second was agitation or aggressive behaviour (33.6%, no difference). Bradycardia was more frequent in Group A (23.5% against 15.7%, P = 0.027). The other 16 features tested did not differ (overall: vomiting 13.6%, anxiety 12.6%, bradypnoea 9.1%, seizures 7.0%, tachypnoea 14.5%, hypotensive episode 2.0%, arrhythmia 0.9%; Table 2); no patient had hyperthermia.
key_findings.note: Percentages in Table 2 are of patients with data for each feature; missing values range from 1.7% to 54.4%.

key_findings.finding: Fig 2 gives unadjusted odds ratios for ethanol co-ingestion for 18 clinical features: only decreased level of consciousness (1.490, 1.029 to 2.158) and bradycardia (0.604, 0.386 to 0.948) exclude 1; intervals for the rarer features, such as hypotensive episode (1.461, 0.306 to 6.968), arrhythmia (0.663, 0.110 to 4.003) and chest pain (1.272, 0.254 to 6.365), are very wide.
key_findings.note: Both interval columns of Fig 2 are headed 95% CI (lower limit); the second column is the upper limit.

key_findings.finding: ED management: any treatment 60.4% against 49.2% (P = 0.011); sedative drugs 20.1% against 12.8% (P = 0.034); no differences in antidotes (naloxone 21.5% against 19%, flumazenil 3.4% in both) or orotracheal intubation (5.3% overall; 5.9% against 3.9%, P = 0.321). Intubation rose as the Glasgow Coma Score fell (0.7% at 15; 2.1% at 8 to 14; 14.5% below 8; P < 0.001) and was not related to vomiting or seizures.

Disposition and stay: 63.9% discharged (389; 66 against medical advice) and 35.9% hospitalised (219), with no overall difference between groups (P = 0.842); among patients hospitalised, critical care 55.3% in Group B against 22.4% in Group A and medical ward 43.4% against 76.1%; median time in hospital 3 h 11 min against 2 h 18 min (P < 0.001); stay over 6 hours 28.4% against 16.9% (P = 0.003).

Deaths: two patients (0.3%), both in Group B (P = 1.00): a 35-year-old man with an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, intubated and ventilated by paramedics, who died in the ED despite resuscitation, and a 32-year-old man with an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, return of circulation after resuscitation, admission to intensive care, hypoxic ischaemic brain injury on CT, and care withdrawn 2 days later to allow organ donation. The author notes mortality may be higher, as deaths outside hospital and direct admissions to intensive care are not in the registry.

Discussion: co-ingestion of ethanol is associated with significant differences in clinical features, generally leading to greater severity (more reduced consciousness, more treatment, more critical care admission, longer stay); agitation may reflect low doses early on or recovery; vomiting (13%) was less frequent than in earlier series (mean 23%); no difference in intubation, which the author says may be biased towards a lower rate because other drugs were excluded; level of consciousness, not seizures or vomiting, leads to intubation.

Limits stated: the reference populations may not represent the consumption habits of each city or country; more than 90% of presentations came from six EDs; the context (for example chemsex) was not analysed; patients managed by prehospital services and not brought to an ED are not included; toxicology in 38 patients (6.2%), only in a minority of centres, detecting GHB/GBL in 28.9%; unreported co-ingested drugs cannot be excluded; low frequencies of some features may hide differences (beta error).

Conclusions: the results provide first evidence of the influence of ethanol on the clinical profile of patients who used GHB/GBL, with significant differences in depth of depression of consciousness, need for treatment, admission to the ICU and length of ED stay, all higher with ethanol. No competing interests declared; the Euro-DEN network was funded by a European Commission grant in 2013 to 2015.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Declaration of interests; Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract labels the ages Group A/B 31.5/33.1, the reverse of Table 2 (A 33.1, B 31.5); gives consciousness and sedatives as B/A while the other pairs are A/B; and gives P = 0.031 for consciousness where Results and Table 2 give 0.034.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the Abstract cannot be read pair by pair without the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The critical care percentages in the Abstract (22.4% and 55.3%) are shares of patients hospitalised (15 of 67 and 84 of 152), not of all patients in each group (8.2% and 19.7%, editors' calculation); the Abstract does not give the denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read without the denominator, the figures overstate how many patients needed critical care.

reporting_issues.issue: The Highlights and Conclusions say ethanol co-ingestion increases adverse effects, but all comparisons are unadjusted; the groups differ in age, arrival by ambulance and probably centre (the share with ethanol ranges from 54% to 86% across the six large centres), and ethanol status rests on report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The differences are associations; a causal increase is the author's reading, supported by physiology but not shown by the design.

reporting_issues.issue: Depth of depression of consciousness is claimed, but only the share with a Glasgow Coma Score below 13 is compared, 58 patients (9.5%) are missing, and the timing of the score is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether consciousness was more deeply depressed (not only more often below the cut-off) is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: About 33 between-group comparisons are reported without correction for multiplicity; the main clinical difference, reduced consciousness, has P = 0.034 and an interval whose lower limit is 1.029.
reporting_issues.consequence: One or two of the eight differences reported as significant may be chance; consciousness would not survive a Bonferroni correction (editors' note).

reporting_issues.issue: No difference in intubation (5.9% against 3.9%, P = 0.321) and in slow breathing (8.2% against 11.6%; 20.7% of breathing rates missing) is reported, and the Discussion explains the intubation result by the exclusion of other drugs; the intervals are wide (intubation odds ratio about 1.5, about 0.7 to 3.7, editors' rough calculation) and no oxygen saturation, arterial gas or airway outcome other than intubation is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not show that ethanol leaves breathing unaffected; it shows that a difference was not detected in this unadjusted, incomplete comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 and the Results give 19.9% of discharged patients as leaving against medical advice; 66 of 389 is 17.0% (editors' calculation), and 19.9% is close to Group A's 19.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A transcription error of no consequence for the ethanol comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text gives the share of admitted patients going to conventional wards as 77.6% (Group A) and 44.7% (Group B); Table 3 gives 76.1% (51 of 67) and 43.4% (66 of 152), which the printed counts reproduce.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small text-table mismatch in the complement of the critical care share; the table values are used here, and the critical care shares (22.4% and 55.3%) agree in text and table.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions say the results are the first evidence of the influence of ethanol on patients who used GHB/GBL, but the reference list includes earlier clinical series with concomitant alcohol and drug use (Liechti 2006; Miro 2017) and omits the controlled experiment of ethanol with GHB in volunteers (Thai 2006).
reporting_issues.consequence: Novelty is overstated; the earlier controlled study measured a different outcome (oxygen saturation) at fixed amounts.

verification.source_read: PDF Galicia_2019_EthanolCoingestionGHB.pdf (the journal's accepted manuscript, 16 pages; not the typeset article, so cited by section and paragraph, counted in running text), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout. Read: highlights, abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 3, Figs 1 and 2, references and declaration of interests. Tables 1 to 3 and Figs 1 and 2 were checked on rendered pages (counts by centre add to 609; Fig 1 flow adds up; Fig 2 odds ratios read from the printed column); discussion paragraphs were checked on the rendered pages.
